articles.title: Jo Adell and José Ramírez star as the Guardians beat the White Sox 9-3 to avoid elimination
articles.summary: Adell’s three-run triple gave Cleveland a 4-1 lead in the third inning. Ramírez’s triple drove in Travis Bazzana and Patrick Bailey for a 7-3 advantage in the eighth.
articles.body: Jo Adell and José Ramírez powered Cleveland with a pair of two-out triples, and the Guardians avoided an AL Division Series sweep by cooling off the Chicago White Sox with a 9-3 victory in Game 3 on Wednesday. Adell’s three-run triple gave Cleveland a 4-1 lead in the third inning. Ramírez’s three-bagger drove in Travis Bazzana and Patrick Bailey for a 7-3 advantage in the eighth. The Guardians recorded two triples in a postseason game for the first time in franchise history. They became the first major league team to accomplish the feat since the Los Angeles Dodgers in Game 1 of the 2024 World Series. Adell, Ramírez, Bailey and Brayan Rocchio each had two of the team’s 11 hits — a complete turnaround for the AL Central champions after they managed just three runs and seven hits in the first two games of the series combined. Game 4 is Thursday. Chicago won its first four games in a surprising postseason appearance after going 60-102 last year. It was backed by a frenzied crowd of 40,590 for the franchise’s first home playoff game since 2021, but there wasn’t much for the fans to cheer in the final innings. The White Sox struck out 19 times and went 2 for 11 with runners in position. Their bullpen faltered after coming up big in their fast postseason start. Chicago jumped in front on Kyle Teel’s RBI double off Daniel Espino with one out in the first. But Espino fanned Chase Meidroth before Foster Griffin struck out Tristan Peters looking, stranding runners on second and third. Griffin set a franchise record for a reliever with seven strikeouts in 2 2/3 innings. The left-hander allowed one run and two hits. Cleveland rallied in the third against Bryan Hudson, who entered after Sean Newcomb pitched two scoreless innings. Bazzana walked and scored on Steven Kwan’s one-out single to left. Facing left-hander Hagen Smith with two down and the bases loaded, Adell grounded a high fastball down the first-base line for a 4-1 lead. Adell, who was acquired in an August trade with the Los Angeles Angels, also hit an RBI triple during Cleveland’s 4-3 loss in Game 2. He hit one triple during the regular season in each of the last two years. Playing in his 48th postseason game — all with Cleveland — Ramírez manufactured an insurance run for the Guardians in the fifth. He doubled, stole third and scored on Chase DeLauter’s grounder to second, beating Teel’s tag with a headfirst slide. Ramírez’s savvy baserunning gave the Guardians a 5-2 lead. The seven-time All-Star went 0 for 6 with two walks in the first two games of the series.

images.caption: Jo Adell #7 of the Cleveland Guardians slides into third base with a triple in the third inning during Game Three of the American League Division Series presented by Booking.com between the Cleveland Guardians and the Chicago White Sox at Rate Field on Wednesday, October 7, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois.

articles.title: Updated MLB Playoff Bracket Picture 2026 After Yankees, Braves, Padres Eliminated
articles.summary: The Los Angeles Dodgers advanced beyond the National League Division Series with a 4-1 win over the Atlanta Braves in Game 4 on Wednesday night.
articles.body:
The Los Angeles Dodgers advanced beyond the National League Division Series with a 4-1 win over the Atlanta Braves in Game 4 on Wednesday night.

Shohei Ohtani and the Dodgers now await the Milwaukee Brewers, which advanced to the NLCS after eliminating the San Diego Padres.

In the American League, the Tampa Bay Rays secured a series sweep over the New York Yankees with a 4-3 victory in Game 3 of the ALDS.

Meanwhile, the Cleveland Guardians kept the team's season alive with a Game 3 win over the Chicago White Sox in their series.

Game 4: Cleveland at Chicago (8 p.m. ET, TBS)

Game 5 (if necessary): Chicago at Cleveland (8 p.m. ET, TBS)

Atlanta struck first on Wednesday and the Braves looked like they would keep their season alive after Michael Harris II scored on a wild pitch by Tyler Glasnow to give his team a 1-0 lead in the bottom of the first inning.

The Dodgers quickly responded in the top of the second, as a pair of errors from Sean Murphy and Mauricio Dubón allowed Ohtani to round the bases and tie the score at 1-1.

With the bases loaded and two outs, Andy Pages hit a single to give the Dodgers a 3-1 advantage.

Max Muncy eventually provided Los Angeles with some insurance in the top of the ninth inning, launching a solo home run to right field. It was enough to secure the 3-1 series lead.

In the other NLDS, the Brewers were simply too much for the Padres in all phases of the game.

Manny Machado did give San Diego a glimmer of hope with a potential game-tying home run in the 8th inning, but Garrett Mitchell robbed it at the wall to keep the score at 3-1:

The Padres never got another chance and were eliminated in the four-game series.

The Yankees didn't even get a win in their series, suffering a sweep at the hands of the Rays.

Victor Mesa Jr. gave Tampa the lead with a sixth-inning two-run home run. Anthony Volpe seemingly tied it in the bottom of the inning, but a fan interference call kept the Rays ahead:

Tampa held on to complete the three-game sweep over New York and advance to the ALCS to face either the Cleveland Guardians or Chicago White Sox.

articles.title: Cleveland Guardians finally find some offense, keep their season alive in ALDS Game 3. vs White Sox
articles.summary: The Guards extended their season at least one more day with a 9-3 victory over Chicago.
articles.body:
CHICAGO — The task was pretty simple for the Cleveland Guardians going into Game 3 of the ALDS: Win or be swept. With the Chicago White Sox holding a 2-0 series lead, going on the road added to the challenge for the Guardians.

In order to stave off elimination and fight back in this series, Cleveland was going to have to find some offense to match a red-hot White Sox team. And to silence a raucous crowd at Rate Field, the Guardians would need to put runs on the board early.

Well, the Guardians were up to the challenge Wednesday. They scored runs early and often in Game 3, routing the White Sox 9-3 to keep their season alive and force a Game 4 on Thursday.

"I think pressure is external," Guardians manager Stephen Vogt said. "You only feel the pressure you put on yourself. So we had pressure today. It's win or go home."

Offense is not the Guardians' strength; they ranked just 24th in MLB in runs scored this season. And through the first two games of this ALDS, big hits had been awfully hard to come by.

Cleveland didn't put much pressure on the White Sox in those two games, going 0-for-8 with runners in scoring position. Not only were the Guardians not creating much traffic, but even when they did, they weren't driving in runs.

But the third inning of Game 3 offered the Guardians a golden opportunity to rally. A leadoff walk followed by two one-out singles tied the game 1-1. Then White Sox rookie Hagen Smith walked José Ramírez to load the bases.

Another out put the Guardians in danger of wasting their bases-loaded opportunity. But after finding some offense late in Game 2, Guardians designated hitter Jo Adell carried that success into Game 3. On a 1-2 count, Adell lined a high fastball from Smith down the right-field line, and it slowly rolled to the wall, clearing the bases and giving the Guardians a 4-1 lead. It was Adell's second triple in as many games.

"It felt like a big, deep breath that we were able to take," left fielder Steven Kwan said afterward. "I feel like the first couple games, we were getting the baserunners on. [But] we didn't get the big hit. Got the big hit there — it definitely felt good."

When the Guardians acquired Adell from the Angels at the trade deadline, the idea was to provide additional impact for a lineup that needed it. And when his moment came in Game 3, the DH delivered.

"I think anytime we're in a position where we're able to put early pressure, we're looking to take advantage," Adell said of the Guardians' third inning. "This is the postseason. There's matchups all the way through — the first inning all the way into the ninth. So we know when we can get ahead and get some traffic, it's really, really crucial to get those runs up early."

Cleveland's four-run third inning was monumental for a few reasons. It saved the Guardians' season, at least for a day. Also, innings like that haven't happened often this season for the Guardians. Cleveland scored four or more runs in an inning just 26 times in the 2026 regular season, which ranked 29th in MLB. Only the Texas Rangers had fewer big innings.

On Wednesday, Cleveland's success at the plate didn't stop in the third inning. The Guardians continued to put pressure on the White Sox's pitchers, as they consistently got on base, drawing a total of 10 walks in the contest to go with 11 hits while handing Chicago its first loss of the postseason.

Ten different Guardians recorded a hit and/or scored a run in the 9-3 rout. Four players — Adell, Patrick Bailey, Brayan Rocchio and Ramírez — recorded multi-hit games.

Amid all the fireworks from Cleveland's victory, Ramírez's big game — 2-for-4 with a double, triple, walk and stolen base — might be one of the biggest developments for the Guardians and could be exactly what they needed as they try to force a Game 5 in this series.

"I don't think anybody's surprised. That's just what he does and what he can do at all times," Kwan said postgame. "When we get all excited for him, he tells everybody, 'Why are you surprised? This is what I do.'"

That might be so, but the Guardians' superstar third baseman did not have the kind of MVP-caliber season the baseball world has come to expect from him. Much of that likely has to do with the hamate bone fracture he sustained in early June, an injury from which it often takes hitters six months to fully recover.

But Ramírez looked like his old self in Game 3. He also showed his all-around skills defensively, snagging a Miguel Vargas line drive that would've tied the game in the sixth inning.

"We always know he's one swing away," Vogt said. "When he hit that first ball in the first inning — the lineout, great play by [Randal] Grichuk — you knew he was here. He creates a run with his legs. That's why he's one of the best players in the league. He can hurt you with the bat, the legs and the glove. He showed all that today."

The Guardians still face elimination Thursday but they clearly believe they've at the very least swung momentum back in their favor. In addition to finding their groove on offense, they have their two aces, Parker Messick and Gavin Williams, lined up for Game 4 on Thursday and a potential Game 5 on Saturday.

"We came here to compete," Ramírez said. "That's what they did also … they won two games. We can do it, too.

"Our mindset is the same: Just come here tomorrow, win one more game, and keep going."

articles.title: Anthony Volpe homer downgraded to double on clear fan interference call at Yankee Stadium
articles.summary: Some Yankees fans responded by pelting the field with trash.
articles.body:
Anthony Volpe had a game-tying home run — at least until the umpires looked at what happened at the left-field wall.

With the New York Yankees down 4-2 in the sixth inning of ALDS Game 3 and trying to avoid a sweep at the hands of the Tampa Bay Rays, shortstop Anthony Volpe clubbed a 357-foot fly ball that left fielder Victor Mesa Jr. couldn't grab. Mesa immediately signaled for the umpires to intervene after the play, while the fan who caught the ball euphorically celebrated a tie game with his peers.

Replay soon showed what happened. The Yankees fan had reached over the wall to catch the ball, which would have clearly stayed in the park without help. The umpires soon ruled fan interference on the play, downgrading the hit to a double.

The play still resulted in a run for the Yankees, but Volpe was sent back to second base and was later stranded on a Spencer Jones strikeout to end the inning, with the Rays still leading 4-3. The Rays hung on to win and advanced to the ALCS , in which they'll face the winner of the Cleveland Guardians-Chicago White Sox series in the other ALDS.

Here's MLB's official ex planation on the play in the Bronx:

"After viewing all relevant angles, the Replay Official definitively determined the spectator interfered with the ball over the field of play. The ball would not have left the playing field nor would it have been caught. The call is OVERTURNED, there was spectator interference and no home run. Additionally, the Replay Official scored one run and placed the batter-runner at second."

It was the correct call. It was the obvious call. It still wasn't popular with the Yankee Stadium fans, some of whom responded by throwing various items onto the field.

Mesa later had his fun with the jeering fans.

This is the second straight series in which a fan caught a ball they arguably shouldn't have, as the Boston Red Sox avoided a similar fate on a Willson Contreras long ball in the wild-card series .

And, of course, this play echoes the infamous Jeffrey Maier play in the 1996 ALCS, with the opposite outcome. In that case, the young Maier caught a fly ball from the Yankees shortstop, Derek Jeter, but the umpires declined to help the Baltimore Orioles.

Friday will mark the 30th anniversary of that play.

images.caption: Yankees fans reached a little too far during Game 3 against the Rays. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect / REUTERS)

articles.title: Victor Mesa Jr., Rays hang on in Game 3 to complete sweep over Yankees, reach ALCS
articles.summary: The Rays are headed back to the ALCS for the first time since 2020.
articles.body: Victor Mesa Jr. knew immediately on Wednesday. He didn't even watch the ball go out of Yankee Stadium. Instead, he turned to get the celebration started with his dugout. And it was well deserved.Mesa and the Tampa Bay Rays held on late, even after a clear fan interference call, to beat the New York Yankees 4-3 on Wednesday in ALDS Game 3. That gave them a series sweep and sent them to the American League Championship Series for the first time since their World Series run in 2020.THE RAYS ARE ALCS-BOUND FOR THE FIRST TIME SINCE 2020 🔥 pic.twitter.com/m7SUTWCMdT— TNT Sports U.S. (@TNTSportsUS) October 8, 2026 While the game was tight early — the Yankees kept pace with the Rays after an RBI single from Jonathan Aranda in the third and a solo homer from Ryan Vilade in the fourth — it was Mesa who blew the game open. After Junior Caminero reached base in the sixth on a single to center, Mesa destroyed a 77-mph slider from Max Fried. And instead of watching his shot, or even starting to run a little bit, he just turned toward the dugout. Victor Mesa Jr. took a moment after his home run 🥶 pic.twitter.com/Hmy7DNUBeW— MLB (@MLB) October 8, 2026 The ball went more than 400 feet and had no issue clearing the wall for his first career postseason home run. That put the Rays up 4-2.It looked like the Yankees tied the game in the bottom of the inning when Anthony Volpe appeared to hit a two-run shot of his own. But that was downgraded to a double after clear fan interference at the left-field wall. Volpe's ball clearly would've stayed in the park without help.After replay review, the Yankees pull within a run on Anthony Volpe's RBI double! pic.twitter.com/6Fua0LNVBQ— MLB (@MLB) October 8, 2026 Officials gave the Yankees one run, ruling that Mesa would not have caught the ball even if it had stayed in the park, which kept the Rays ahead 4-3. Mesa got into it with Yankees fans after the play. Some Yankees fans threw trash down onto the field after the replay, which delayed the game momentarily.Victor Mesa Jr. going at it with Yankees fans in left field after the big call in the 7th inning 😅 pic.twitter.com/OwtivL3SoU— B/R Walk-Off (@BRWalkoff) October 8, 2026 That took all of the air out of the New York crowd. The Yankees couldn't get anything going in the next two frames while the Rays held their lead, and then Bryan Baker came in to wrap things up on the mound for Tampa Bay in the ninth. Volpe struck out swinging to open the inning, and the Rays nearly ended the series on a double play off a Jazz Chisholm grounder. Baker ultimately struck out Trent Grisham to secure the victory.The Rays will head to the ALCS for the third time in franchise history. The past two times, they reached the World Series. They'll await the winner of the ALDS between the Chicago White Sox and Cleveland Guardians. The Guardians won 9-3 in their Game 3 matchup earlier Wednesday to force a Game 4. The Yankees, meanwhile, will head to the offseason having fallen in the ALDS for a second straight year. They didn't lead for a single moment in this series. And now their hopes of a second World Series trip in the past three years are over.

articles.title: Ronald Acuña Jr. flails as Braves fall to Dodgers, and difficult questions are coming in Atlanta: 'I did nothing to help the team'
articles.summary: Atlanta's offense all but disappeared in the final two games of its NLDS loss to LA.
articles.body:
ATLANTA — The face of Atlanta's postseason collapse sat in a corner of the Braves' locker room, blue dri-fit shirt pulled tight over his bowed head. All around Ronald Acuña Jr., the pops and slaps of hugs and daps resounded in the quiet locker room, marking the many farewells of a season that had ended earlier than anyone wanted.

The Braves whimpered out of the postseason on Wednesday , surrendering a second straight winnable game to the Dodgers in Atlanta after splitting the first two in Los Angeles. Losing in the postseason isn't unusual for Atlanta — or, at this point, for any team not based in Los Angeles — but the way Atlanta went out, meek and flailing, will sting.

"That's the postseason. You never know what you're going to get," Braves manager Walt Weiss said shortly after the final out. "You have a lot of unsung heroes a lot of times in the postseason, and sometimes guys struggle. It's obviously magnified because you're playing under a microscope."

That's true, but you didn't need a microscope to see the Braves' struggles in their final two games; they were visible from orbit. Zero-for-11 with men in scoring position. Sixteen men left on base. Opportunity after opportunity squandered time after time.

Acuña wasn't the only Brave to struggle at the plate in this series — he had two inconsequential singles in 15 at-bats — but he was the most visible one, given that he's the franchise's unquestioned star and the guy whose No. 13 jersey outnumbers all the others in the Truist Park stands.

"It's really frustrating. To say I'm disappointed would be an understatement," Acuña said via an interpreter after the game. "I'm particularly frustrated with myself. I feel like I did nothing to help the team this series. I'm supposed to be a spark plug for my team out there, and I never lit that fire. Extremely disappointed, very frustrated."

All four times Acuña walked to the plate in Game 4, a Brave was on base. All four times he failed to bring them home — striking out twice, walking once and, in his final at-bat of the season, grounding out to end the Braves' final scoring opportunity.

That final, meek out — coming on the very first pitch he saw, with Michael Harris II standing on second and the Braves trailing by two runs in the bottom of the seventh — brought out something that longtime observers of the Braves couldn't recall ever hearing before: boos for a Brave. They weren't thunderous, anti-Freddie-Freeman-level boos … but they weren't isolated, either, and they weren't shy.

Acuña heard the boos and accepted them. "It's really frustrating because they're well within their rights to boo and to say what they think and feel," he said later. "I didn't do anything [to help the team]."

He wasn't alone. Outside of Harris, every Braves batter who stepped to the plate this series might as well have been swinging a toothbrush. Matt Olson: 2-for-16. Drake Baldwin: 1-for-14. Austin Riley: 0-for-14. Ozzie Albies: 3-for-15. At least Albies' hits were two doubles and a home run.

"The Dodgers have something to do with [the Braves' offensive woes]," Weiss said afterward. "They're going for their third straight world championship for a reason. Their arms just keep coming at you."

Given what the Braves went through this season — wracked with injuries, setting out with a new skipper, stumbling into the playoffs with just two starting pitchers — it's arguable that this Braves team overachieved. This NLDS marked the first time Atlanta advanced past its first round of the postseason since 2021, the year the team won the World Series, and just the fourth time overall in the 2000s.

But achievement creates expectation, and this team proved — with its 5-1 record against the Dodgers in the regular season, its early-season surge, its late-season sprint and its gutsy elimination-game win against Philadelphia in the wild-card round — that it has the potential to achieve greatness. Now come the questions about whether this core, as currently constituted, can capitalize on that potential and advance past the divisional round.

In the top of the ninth inning Wednesday, perhaps to engender a little goodwill with the nearby fans, Acuña tossed his last warm-up ball of the season into the stands along the first-base line. It's not impossible that someone wearing an Acuña jersey caught it; there were hundreds, maybe thousands of them in the stands at every game this season.

Acuña won Atlanta fans' love with his magnificent early-career performances — his 2018 grand slam against these same Dodgers in the NLCS, his home run on the first pitch he saw in 2025 after nearly a full year lost to injury, his 40/70 season in 2023 that led to his unanimous MVP.

Starting next year, though, he'll need to work at getting them to believe in him — and the rest of the Braves' bats — all over again.

articles.title: The L.A. Dodgers, self-proclaimed 'dinosaurs,' are moving on to the NLCS once again after dispatching the Braves
articles.summary: The Dodgers' aging core of stars didn't perform at their best in the NLDS vs. Atlanta, but it was enough for yet another champagne celebration.
articles.body:
ATLANTA — For at least the 30th time in the past 10 years, Dave Roberts addressed a crowd of hulking, goggled men eager to douse one another in booze.

As the Dodgers manager lavished deserved praise on his victorious ballclub, the 54-year-old gripped a gold-tipped bottle of bubbly in his left hand. Meanwhile, another 750 milliliters of joy rested snugly in the back pocket of his baseball pants. The Dodgers players weren't the only ones ready to party.

But first, Roberts had some words of affirmation.

"There's no more talented team than the Los Angeles Dodgers," the three-time World Series-winning skipper boasted. "It's the best organization in sports, top to bottom. We're smarter, we're better, and we're tougher."

"And we're dinosaurs!" outfielder Teoscar Hernández, 33, interjected.

The room erupted in laughter, drowning out Roberts. Hernández's self-deprecating quip was a reference to a comment made earlier this season by newly minted San Diego Padres owner José E. Feliciano, who proclaimed, "The owner of the Dodgers owns a lot of dinosaurs." And while the Dodgers' chairman and top dog, Mark Walter, does indeed own a large number of prehistoric animal fossils, Feliciano's remark was interpreted as a slight toward Los Angeles' aging core of position players.

Hernández, Shohei Ohtani, Mookie Betts, Will Smith, Freddie Freeman, Max Muncy, Tommy Edman and Kiké Hernández are all over 30. Freeman is 37. Muncy is 36. Betts turned 34 on Wednesday. Gray hairs, both real and proverbial, are starting to sprout.

"We're old! We're f***ing old, yes," veteran infielder Miguel Rojas, 37 and nursing a back injury, belted over the revelrous din.

The Dodgers dinosaurs dispatched the Atlanta Braves 4-1 on Wednesday in an NLDS Game 4 that felt much more one-sided than that. Granted, the contest hung in the balance for much of the night, as starters Tyler Glasnow and Tyler Mahle traded zeroes after each team scored a sloppy run in the first inning. The score remained knotted at one as Glasnow and Mahle exited the stage, thrusting the bullpens into the spotlight.

Game 2 hero Didier Fuentes entered for Mahle in the seventh with one on and one out. He coaxed Max Muncy into a groundout but promptly issued free passes to the next two Dodgers: Josue De Paula, a 21-year-old with 42 career regular-season plate appearances, and Kyle Tucker, the highest-paid man in MLB history. That brought Atlanta skipper Walt Weiss out of the dugout and flame-throwing reliever Robert Suarez into the game. Up to the dish stepped Los Angeles outfielder Andy Pages, a most fascinating character in the Dodgers extended universe.

Pages, 25, is not old. Had he been born in the U.S. and not Cuba, he might still be on his parents' health insurance. Last autumn, Pages delivered one of the all-time putrid postseason statistical performances, going 4-for-51 with one measly RBI. That earned him a benching for Games 5, 6 and 7 of the World Series, though he more than made up for his lackluster bat with a season-saving snag in that dramatic Game 7.

This season, Pages leveled up as a hitter, earning a spot as the National League's starting center fielder in the All-Star Game. But a late-summer injury derailed his rhythm as October approached. He began this NLDS 0-for-7 with four strikeouts. It looked concerningly familiar. Roberts, though, didn't lose confidence.

"I'm gonna continue to give Andy leash," the skipper said before Game 3. "I believe in him. I feel that for us to win the World Series this year, we're gonna need him to be an active part of our team."

In Game 3, Pages collected two knocks and scored a run. In Game 4, he provided the definitive blow.

With the bases juiced and the count full, Pages roped a 100-mph Suarez heater back up the middle for a two-run, backbreaking single. Teoscar Hernández and pinch runner Edman scurried home. Muncy added a solo shot in the ninth. The Dodgers' bullpen did the rest. Los Angeles, once more, ended an October evening soaked in alcohol and smelling of cigars.

"When you're spraying champagne and beer on everybody, there's nothing cooler than this, man," Muncy said amidst the bacchanal. "You work seven, eight months to get to this point. You gotta take advantage of this. This is why you play baseball."

But not all the Dodgers played good baseball this week, including some of the most important ones, the older ones.

Ohtani went 2-for-13 and did not record an extra-base hit. He looks discombobulated, far from the world-beater we've come to expect. Roberts batted him fifth in Game 3, for goodness' sake. Betts was 3-for-14 with all singles. Catcher Will Smith (1-for-16) looked the worst of the lot. It was far from a reassuring offensive showing. L.A. scored just 3.5 runs per game. The lineup's .264 collective OBP in this NLDS was the lowest mark posted by a 21st-century Dodgers team in a victorious playoff series.

Their relatively comprehensive series victory, then, is a testament to an otherworldly pitching staff. It turns out that a rotation of Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell, Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Tyler Glasnow can win you some low-scoring ballgames. The bullpen, thought to be this club's Achilles' heel, also stepped up to surrender just four earned across 14 2/3 innings of work, including 4 1/3 scoreless to close out Game 4. That's how a club overcomes a .203 team batting average — by holding its opponents to a .145/.259/.242 slash line.

"The Dodgers have something to do with that," Braves manager Walt Weiss said after the game about his team's offensive struggles . "They're going for their third straight world championship for a reason. Their arms just keep coming at you."

And next week, they'll keep on coming in the NLCS. An enticing rematch against a souped-up Brewers team awaits. Milwaukee's lineup is sure to put up a better fight than it did last year and almost certainly a better fight than Atlanta's hitters just mustered. Game 1 will be Sunday in Wisconsin, and it should be a battle.

But that impending showdown was most certainly not front of mind for the Dodgers after their victory Wednesday. Imitation champagne flowed freely. No reporter, player or staff member was safe from a chilly Budweiser shower. Rojas, the elder statesman of this aging empire, bad back and all, bounced around the room with a bright green, $150 bottle of tequila in his hand. He chanted along to the TikTok viral house remix bumping from the locker room speakers.

"Get money, stay pretty, handle your business, enjoy life, stay sexy and don't give a f***."

Quite the mantra for a group of dinosaurs.

articles.title: Magic Johnson Sends Message to Dodgers After NLCS Announcement
articles.summary: Magic Johnson celebrated the Dodgers' latest playoff triumph and highlighted three players who helped send Los Angeles to the NLCS. The post Magic Johnson Se...
articles.body:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are headed back to the National League Championship Series, and team co-owner Magic Johnson wasted little time celebrating.

Following the Dodgers' 4-1 victory over the Atlanta Braves on Wednesday, October 7, Johnson took to X to recognize three players who helped Los Angeles clinch the National League Division Series in four games.

"Another win for my Dodgers!! Two key plays tonight were Max Muncy's home run and Andy Pages' hit to drive in a couple runs and seal the victory for us to advance to the NL Championship Series! I was also impressed with Tyler Glasnow tonight, who gave the Dodgers another great pitching night for the team," Johnson wrote.

His message came after Los Angeles secured its third consecutive appearance in the NLCS, keeping alive its pursuit of a third straight World Series championship.

And while Johnson highlighted the offense, the Dodgers' latest victory was another example of their pitching staff delivering in October.

Magic Johnson Praises Andy Pages, Max Muncy After Dodgers Beat Braves

The Dodgers needed someone to break through with runners in scoring position. Andy Pages finally delivered.

With the game tied in the seventh inning, Pages came through with a two-run single that gave Los Angeles the lead. Remarkably, it was the Dodgers' first hit with runners in scoring position of the entire series.

Max Muncy added a solo home run in the ninth inning to provide insurance, his third homer of the postseason.

Pages finished with two of the Dodgers' five hits and two of their three RBIs.

Tyler Glasnow also earned recognition from Johnson for his outing against Atlanta.

The pitching staff ultimately helped close the door on the Braves, allowing just two hits over the final 4 1/3 innings. Edgardo Henriquez earned the victory, while Edwin Díaz recorded his second save of the series.

Atlanta finished the NLDS just 1-for-23 with runners in scoring position.

When Is the Dodgers' Next Game? 2026 NLCS Schedule and Opponent

The Dodgers' next scheduled game is Sunday, October 11, when Game 1 of the National League Championship Series begins.

Los Angeles will face the winner of the NLDS matchup between the Milwaukee Brewers and San Diego Padres .

The Brewers entered Wednesday's Game 4 with a 2-1 series lead, meaning Milwaukee had an opportunity to clinch the matchup while San Diego was fighting to extend its season.

The Dodgers' NLCS opponent will also determine where the series begins.

If Milwaukee advances, the Dodgers will open the NLCS on the road. If San Diego advances, Los Angeles will host the first game.

Both games are scheduled for FOX or FS1, according to MLB's postseason calendar.

The NLCS, short for National League Championship Series, is a best-of-seven matchup. The winner advances to the World Series to face the American League champion.

Dave Roberts, Dodgers Move Closer to Historic World Series Three-Peat

Johnson's celebration also comes as manager Dave Roberts adds another achievement to his postseason résumé.

With Wednesday's victory, Roberts moved into sole possession of second place in MLB managerial postseason victories with 72, passing Tony La Russa. Only Joe Torre, with 84, has more.

The Dodgers have also won 10 of their last 11 postseason road games and own a 14-5 road record over the past three postseasons.

Los Angeles is now eight victories away from becoming the first National League franchise to win three consecutive World Series championships.

The last MLB team to accomplish a World Series three-peat was the New York Yankees , who won three straight titles from 1998 through 2000.

For the Dodgers, another NLCS appearance represents an opportunity to continue one of baseball's most impressive modern postseason runs.

And after eliminating Atlanta, Johnson has three more names to celebrate as Los Angeles moves another step closer to history.

articles.title: Padres star Manny Machado livid after Garrett Mitchell robs game-tying home run, helping Brewers advance to NLCS
articles.summary: Manny Machado's game-tying home run was so close to clearing the Petco Park wall on Wednesday night.
articles.body:
Manny Machado was so, so close to tying things up on Wednesday night.

But thanks to a wild catch from Garrett Mitchell, the Milwaukee Brewers are headed to the National League Championship Series for a second straight season.

Machado, with the Padres down by two runs in the eighth inning on Wednesday night, hit a deep shot to center field. It looked like a home run instantly. Machado stopped and stared from home plate, and Petco Park erupted with the idea that the game was going to be tied up 3-3.

But Mitchell played it perfectly, and managed to get in front of the ball right at the wall to make the two-handed grab.

"Just got a good read off the bat, got back to the wall as quickly as I could just to get my feet set and made the play," Mitchell said on FS1 after the win. "But great swing by him."

Machado was, understandably, livid. He ripped his helmet off, and was spotted smashing it repeatedly in the dugout.

The photos from Mitchell's catch are incredible, too — and show just how close a group of Padres fans were from actually making an impact on the play. Mitchell, remarkably, cut them off just in time.

While the Padres stopped Milwaukee from adding any more runs in the top of the ninth, Machado's look was their best chance. They failed to tie the game up in the ninth, which ended their season and gave the Brewers the 3-1 win.

Had Machado's home run carried even just a little bit further, and it would have been a very different game. It could have even forced a Game 5 in Milwaukee.

But instead, it's the Brewers who will get to take on the Los Angeles Dodgers in the NLCS with a shot at a World Series trip on the line. Machado and the Padres, thanks to some heroics from Mitchell, are done.

images.caption: Garrett Mitchell robbed a game-tying home run from Manny Machado on Wednesday night to help lift the Brewers to the NLCS. (AP Photo/Gregory Bull)
